utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, we are now in March 1999. In March 1999, before the NATO bombing started, was the VJ in your town, in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the army was present, as was also the police. There were also Serbian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they wear uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army had its own uniform. There were also police and army elite forces. There were the Frenki's men, SAJ, and other paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the army uniform, what colour and any other description you can give us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army had camouflage uniforms. Frenki's men also had camouflage uniforms but a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What colour was the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to see a photograph, I could tell you better.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the witness shown Exhibit 18, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, starting with the army, can you see in the sheet in front of you any uniform that is similar to the ones that the army was using?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the army uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Which number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You said it was also a special police army. Did they wear the same uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's number 8. That was the uniform of the special forces, so-called Frenki's men. That's number 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the uniform of the regular police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You mentioned the SAJ. Can you see any uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's number 6, but there are -- there are no SAJ units here. But it's similar to that, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were there other paramilitary groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were other paramilitary groups belonging to Seselj, what were called the White Eagles. Here it's number 9. These were Serbian paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What were they doing in your town right before the NATO bombing started in March?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, they went out of their barracks and came to the town and sent the people out of their houses by force with their armoured vehicles and cars. They put them among the garages of Albanian houses and in private shops and in private houses belonging to Albanians. I should also mention the places where they were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Before you continue, Witness, you mentioned "they." Who are "they"? The army, the police, the other groups; who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the army, the police and other groups of Yugoslavia -- of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where was the VJ located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Where was the VJ stationed? Did they have a barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army was stationed in the villages of Komogllave, Rakaj, Naruk, and Nerodime, all in Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You said they moved to town and they expelled the villagers. Why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did this in the villages of Komogllave, Rakaj, Nerodime and Naruk.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened to the people of these towns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They sent away the people from these villages and they fled to Skopje and some to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened to you and your family? Did you leave your home as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went and took my family, because the army and the paramilitaries were firing with hand-held mortars at my home, and I decided to take my family and go. I went to the village of Greme.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you join the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also went with my neighbours and other villagers. We wanted to go to Skopje, but in the convoy where we were, the word spread that I was with the Serbian police, and he will play a trick on us. And the convoy started to keep a distance from me, and I didn't have anything to do, so I took my family and went to the village of Rakaj, and there Serbian paramilitaries were, and out of fear, I decided to go back to my own home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid of both sides. I was -- I was afraid of the people who were talking, and I was afraid for my family, but I was also afraid of the paramilitaries who were in Rakaj and whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You came back home. Did you leave again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went home, and after a time I took my family. And I heard from neighbours that the train was travelling for Skopje, and I decided to take my family, and my wife and I went to Skopje. But when we came out at the Ferizaj train station, there were security inspectors of Ferizaj there, and there was Dimitri and Crni, and out of fear that they might do something, I decided to go yet again back home with my wife and my family. And I saw them off, and they went off to Skopje. And there at the station, Crni and Dimitri called me, and we went to a cafe and sat with them in this cafe belonging to SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just before you continue, so your family left to Skopje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. My family went to Skopje as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And you and your wife stayed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. My wife and I stayed at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So after you met Stojkovic and Dimitri in the railway station, you went to a cafe. What did you discuss over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There we discussed, as they put it -- they said that war has now started in Kosova, and now we're going to flee to Greece.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What else did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We also discussed that business that we had in 1998 that I had to carry out and other jobs that Mitic decided.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So did Mitic want you to continue to work for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Then Dimitri and Crni came to my house, and some others, members of the Anti-Terrorist Unit, and Mitic had sent me orders to go to his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So, Witness, after the cafe and you had the conversation with Dimitri and Stojkovic, did you come back home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that point, you knew that Mitic wanted you to continue to do the jobs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I knew that they would want me to do jobs again, but I couldn't get away because, as I say, they had put a watch on the train station and also on the roads that led to Skopje. So there was no way I could get to Skopje without being seen by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So after you came home, you knew that Mitic wanted to talk to you. Did anybody come to your place to pick you up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Crni came, Stojkovic, Dimitri, and other members of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the other members of the Serb police, if they were wearing uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The members of the special units had a camouflage uniform, because in 1999, they joined the police forces, because this was a secret Black Hand organisation, and they joined with the anti-terrorist groups during the war and took part in operations together. They had cars. They had stolen Mercedes. They were cars belonging to Albanians that were stolen during the war. There was a Mercedes and a red BMW, and also a white Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So, Witness, what you're saying is that the Black Hand -- the group Black Hand was working with the special anti-terrorist group, the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During the war, in 1999, they joined and worked together but only their uniforms were different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- there was no difference. The only difference was in the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: But what was that, the colour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the colour. Only the colour. It was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the colour of the Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you say it again? I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What was the colour of the uniform of the Black Hand group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The uniform of the Black Hand group was black.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what about the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the witness shown Exhibit 18 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you see on this sheet the SAJ uniform or the Black Hand uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here there is no Black Hand uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter requests the witness to talk into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you please talk into the microphone and repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no Black Hand uniforms. There's only the SAJ uniform, which is number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, after they picked you up at your place, did you go to Mitic's office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met Mitic in his office, which was in the town, in the Bankkos building, and there they showed me a number of photographs of members of the KLA and other people, and there in Mitic's office there were also two security inspectors, Dragan Jashovic, and also Spaca Spravala, and they wanted me to know -- wanted to know if I knew any of these members of the KLA. And I recognised some of them. And Dragan also knew one of them from Jezerc called Ekrem Baliu, and I knew them but only their first names and I only recognised their faces, and after a time, they gave me a coat and a mask and sent me to a cafe called Pranvera in Ferizaj. This was during the war of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the two security inspectors, were they policemen? Were they working with Mitic to the same police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They worked together, and they were inspectors on -- for political affairs. They belonged to the state security.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: They belonged to the DB?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They said the DB. In Ferizaj SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: You said you were asked to go to this restaurant Pranvera. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me to the Pranvera restaurant where the Serbian police was established with the inspectors, and there was Branko Nedeljkovic as head inspector, and Srecko Doganovic, and Dragan Joka, and Lubisha. He was a deputy commander. And there were some other inspectors there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What were they doing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had also set up a prison in the cafe cellar, and they had people that they arrested in the town and from the village of Racak and other villages, and they took them and put them in the cellar there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What kind of prison was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a kind of prison -- mostly they were looking for people from the village of Racak, because they committed the Racak massacre. And then the NATO bombing started. And after that, they had, out of spite against the villagers of Racak, they would take them to Ferizaj and put them in the cellar and maltreat them and even kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened when you were in the restaurant? What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a person from Ferizaj called Muhamed Bega. He was 50 years old, and they had tied him up there to a chair with handcuffs and they were beating him. This was Dragan Jashovic and Spaca Spravala.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Why were they beating him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently they had information that his son was in the KLA, with the name of Sadik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What did you see there after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them when they took me to the Pranvera cafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, Witness, you are in the Pranvera cafe. And how many people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people there in that cafe cellar. There were more than 20. I also heard from the inspectors that there were two Albanian women there too. There was a well there at the cafe entrance. There were wallets. There were documents belonging to the prisoners, and there they were guarded by two reserve policemen whose faces I knew. They were from Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And were all the people detained in the basement members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not one of them was a member of the KLA. They were civilians whom they caught in the streets and in shops and round about. There was not a single member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So why were they detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They held them because the Serbian police were angry at the villagers of Racak. And as soon as they caught them on the street or if they were from Petrova in Shtime commune, they would take hold of them and they would beat them with baseball bats. And there were also electric cable, and they were beating them. And the -- the police inspectors and the reservists in line, they would maltreat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what happened to these people, and also, do you know what happened to the man that you identified in the photos, the photos that were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to Muhamed Bega, I only saw the inspectors beating him and asking him about his son, where his son was. And he never answered, but later, I don't know what happened to him. And they took me -- took me to the cellar, as I said before, and they put me in a car and a mask so that nobody would recognise me. But I didn't recognise any of them. So I came up out of the cellar again and went.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So you were -- Witness, you were taken -- you were put in -- you were given a mask, and you were taken into the cellar in order to recognise any person that belonged to the KLA? That's what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as a member of the KLA but -- but in case was any member of the family, any son or daughter -- any son, in case any of them had a member of the family in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you know if these people, if they were released after?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any more what happened to them. I have no information on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to the work that you're doing to Mitic, did Mitic discuss with you again starting to continue to do the tasks you started again in 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went along with that business of 1998. And he added some other jobs for 1999. He started when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So was -- was it the same list that you were discussing during 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same list, but some had been added. Other people and other buildings had been added.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What kind of new targets were added?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new tasks added were places where the buildings where the OSCE had stayed in 1998, they had been noted as buildings to be burnt, and explosives were to be planted there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, were you provided with a uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have a uniform. I only had a coat and a mask.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: A weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a weapon. I had an .88 pistol with a permit from Mitic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How many people were working with you in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a lot of people. There were 15 to 20 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were -- well, I couldn't know their names, but I would know them from photographs. There was Dragan Stojkovic, known as Crni, Dimitri, a policeman called Dzira from Babus. I mentioned Dimitri with the pseudonym Van Damme, and many others, I would know them from photographs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were they members of the Black Hand or the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the Black Hand and of the SAJ, but in the 1999 war, the two groups joined together and worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they have cars and weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had cars, weapons, and they had armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can you describe the cars?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had -- as I said before, there was a Mercedes, a red BMW, and a white 101. There were police jeeps. There was an armoured vehicle. They also had weapons, automatic with silencers, pistols, 15 CZs. They also had knives and M53 automatic rifles and other equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the witness shown Exhibit 17 and 21, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Starting with the vehicles, can you show the Court any of the vehicles you mentioned, if you see them on the sheet.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here there are no photographs of what we're looking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can the usher please show all the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not here. There was an armoured vehicle like this one, number 9. And a jeep, number 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the weapons, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one like number 1 here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The other photos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, none of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the weapon in number 1 photo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an automatic rifle, M45.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. What did Mitic instruct you to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mitic told me to go with the above-mentioned people to work, to set up -- to do work against people who had shown resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember what was your first work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first work was to go to Agim Ibrahimi in Ferizaj, in the new neighbourhood, to go to his house, and we went there. We had three cars with us, and Mitic ordered him to be killed because he was a patriot. He was an Albanian patriot, and the police were afraid of him. They mentioned him quite often. And so we were given orders to go and murder him. So we went there --

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and we killed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, you went to the house of Agim Ibrahimi in 1998 and you did not kill him or liquidate him. You were asked to come back in 1999 and do the job again. What happened in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999, we went back by car. We went to his house, and Dimitri went out and the other members there at his house, Dimitri and another policeman who was with a mask and black clothes and a rifle and a silencer. And there were two dogs there in front of the door. We broke in the door and went in. And ten minutes later, they came out of his house and talked -- spoke on the walkie-talkie with Mitic and said what had been done. I didn't hear what exactly happened to the person because I was outside in the car.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you hear shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard shots, but they were with a silencer. I could -- I just heard when they killed the dogs first.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember a man called Izet Beqiri?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a Yzdri Beqiri.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. Was he on the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yzdri Beqiri was a member of the LDK for Ferizaj in Kosova, and he had a house. In his house were schoolrooms for Albanian children, and orders were given for his house to be burnt down; like, explosives to be planted and the house to be burnt.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And was the job done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. We went and we planted the explosives there with the Serb police organisation, and we blew it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened to the Motel Gimi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Motel Gimi, Mitic had heard that the son of Agimi, who was called Fadil, had become a member of the KLA, and so for this reason we were told to plant explosives at his home and blow it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The members of the special forces, special units, did the job, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: How did they do it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to the hotel twice because the first time we couldn't -- the first time we were there with an armoured vehicle and cars - Mercedes, BMW and the other car - and there were a lot of people around, and fire was opened. They opened fire. Then people were frightened and started running away and -- so we -- because we didn't want anyone to see what was going on. But there were still people at the motel. And they began shooting, and we saw people falling. There were shots, but they were still alive, wounded. They fell to the ground. So they went into the building and planted the explosives and blew up the motel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: So were they shooting at the people outside and inside the hotel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not inside. It was only around out on the street that they were shooting, because there were people out on the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened to the motel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, explosives were planted, but the work didn't -- the job didn't go off well. So we had to go back the second time. I was in the car, and that time they planted the explosives, gas, gasoline, took gasoline inside and blew it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember a man who was a solicitor in Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a solicitor in Ferizaj. Avdulseljami, who was in the Lagjja e Re neighbourhood or street in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And was he on the list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was on the list. We were -- he was supposed to be killed. Mitic had given an order for him to be liquidated. And if he were not there, we were supposed to take his daughter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went with them to his house. We had three cars with us, a Mercedes, the BMW, and the third car. And Dimitri and two or three other people went in from the police. We were all together. They went in and waited for five minutes, ten minutes, maybe. But -- well, Dimitri and the others stayed in the house, and the rest of us, we went back to Bankkos, to the headquarters, where the police headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him or his daughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never found out what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you know at least if the report -- the job was reported as done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened, no. I don't know whether it was done or not. I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, in 1998, you went to -- you testified that you went to the house of Osman Nuha. Did you go back in 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In 1998, there was an order given to go to his village, to the house of Osman Nuha, to the village of Nerodime. So I went with Stojkovic and this guy who had the pseudonym Crni. We had Chinese hand rockets, and we went to the village there, to the police station in Nerodime, and there an order was given -- or Crni was given an order to throw a bomb into the house of Osman Nuha, and the second bomb was for the house of Shaban. And he threw the bomb into Osman Nuha's house and the second into Shaban's house and then we returned and went back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: This was in 1998. And in 1999, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In 1999, I went with them because Mitic didn't like this guy because he was a patriot, and the Serbs don't like them, and they don't like -- mutually they don't like one another, didn't like one another. So an order was given that this person be liquidated, to be killed. Dimitri was -- got the order, and his people from the special unit were given this order to kill him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And with a yes or no, did you do that? Did you or Dimitri or any other person of the group, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do that job. It was Dimitri who did it with the other people. I only accompanied them. I didn't really see what happened, so I don't know. I just heard later them talking on the walkie-talkie, Dimitri, from the car, and was asked what happened, and they said, "Well, there's a lot of blood." There was a knife. They had gloves and masks. So I don't know what happened inside. I just heard the screaming of the women and the children. I was quite a ways away and sitting in the car, so I don't know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, there was a house that was used by Mother Theresa organisation that was in a hospital. Do you remember what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It was the house of Remzi Beqiri in Ferizaj. It was a health centre to help the Albanians. He was the brother of Yzdri Beqiri. The Serb policemen didn't like him for this reason. And so explosives were planted. The two houses were quite -- side by side, so his house was destroyed too and the health centre in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, there was a motel called Sokoli that was the OSCE residence for a while. What happened to this motel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this building in the Zejenl Hajdini Street was where the OSCE had its headquarters, and in 1999, an order was given to bomb it because the observers of the OSCE had been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And with a yes or no, was it bombed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: What happened to a man called Ilmi Recica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. They were -- the Serb police was afraid of him too. They -- Mitic and the other inspectors spoke about him quite often as a dangerous person and that he should be liquidated with members of his family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Ilmi Recica, who was politically -- had been politically convicted earlier for political reasons, because he was a patriot. And so the police had him under observation. And during the war, he was a commander of the KLA for -- in the village of Jezerc. And an order was given that his house be blown up, be mined and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And again with a yes or no, did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And was Ilmi Recica also the head of the Human Rights and Freedom Council?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Earlier, in about 1990 he was, and then later he joined the KLA and was a commander of the UCK -- of the KLA later.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Who is Isufi Ademi and what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the village of Rakaj, and his family had had problems with the Serb police earlier. They had been looking for arms, the police had been looking for arms from his family. And to find a solution, he agreed to work, just to save his family, to work with them. And later on, there was information that this person had fled and joined the KLA and so an order was given to go and murder him and his family, his brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went with the armoured vehicle, with the jeep, and a BMW, and a Mercedes and the other car. We went to the village of Rakaj. We surrounded the house of the person in question in Rakaj. At the start -- he had four dogs in the courtyard, and we shot at them, and we shot at the house. Dimitri shot at the house. And there were no dogs inside the house. And so we set the house on fire, six or seven houses and the garage and all the buildings around, and burnt everything down.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: To whom belonged the six houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those belonged to his brothers, as I said, his brothers, his cousins, family members. They were all burnt down, the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, what happened to Fari Mahalla?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order given to plant explosives in the house of Fari Mahalla and blow it up because they had heard that this person had been financing the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And with a yes or no, did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember any other job that you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't do the other jobs myself. It was the Serb police who did it, like used force. They did a lot of other things. A lot of other houses were blown up. Nezir Maqiteva, his house and other houses in the -- a lot of other houses. Nezir Maqiteva.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did they liquidate anybody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. As far as I would know -- as far as I was there, no. But there was a lot of plundering by paramilitaries of houses. Crni and his people took part in the plundering of a couple of houses, and there were other paramilitary units involved in plundering.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, right before the NATO forces arrived in June 1999, did Mitic contact you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand the question. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: I'll make another question. I'll go to another area first. Do you remember a fight in Kacanik between the KLA and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a fight. I was there at the time when the KLA was fighting the special units of Serbia. We were in the village of Rakaj. From Kacanik, the special units were called by radio to come and assist, because they were being -- had been surrounded by the KLA. And Mitic was asked by walkie-talkie to go, and we so we went to Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And what happened to the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went, we found that a police vehicle had been destroyed. It was a green-coloured vehicle, and two policemen had been wounded. One was called Zuti from Shtime and the other I didn't know. And special forces then came in and took the wounded people away. And the fighting broke out with the KLA, between the KLA and the special forces. And there was a big -- quite a battle. When it got dark, the army came in, the normal Yugoslav army, with tanks and with Praga vehicles, and there were paramilitary units with police inspectors, Serbs. There was one called Novica who took part in the action. He was with the army and the Serb paramilitaries. They accompanied us with tanks and Praga vehicles to the -- back to the police station in Ferizaj then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, did Mitic ever mention to you targeting civilians, killing civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did say -- he did talk about killing civilians when we went to Rakaj. In Rakaj and Nerodime.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you remember, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said -- as I mentioned before, he told me to go to Rakaj and kill Isuf and his brothers and other menfolk that were there. And I also heard the police in Kacanik say that the policemen of Ferizaj were asking whether there was civilians in the town of Kacanik, and they asked why, and they said, Why have you left them there? Why are they not killed?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Turning back to the question that I made before, right before the NATO forces arrived in June 1999, did Mitic contact you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the NATO forces came, Mitic called me up by phone and told me to escape from home and to take my wife, but I didn't want to do this. I was also afraid that they might, in the end, kill me. (redacted) (redacted) there in the yard. And I hid there in a pit like a well until morning, and then they surrounded the house, and they were masked, and they were looking for me, and they looked for me, but they didn't find me. And then about 5.00 in the morning, I changed my place. I went to another house belonging to an uncle in a different neighbourhood, and then I hid myself well and waited until dark, until the Serbian army and police went away. And then I saw NATO helicopters entering. And I came out and went home when they had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, who were looking after you, the Serbs or the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I escaped, I was running away from the Serbs, because I didn't want to go with them to Serbia. And I was also frightened that they were -- I was also frightened that they would kill me, so I hid myself until they went away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you afraid also that the KLA was looking for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was afraid. And I thought the KLA also came to question me, and I was at my uncle's house. And four inspectors in plainclothes belonging to the KLA came. I didn't know their names but I recognised their faces. And they came to my uncle's house where I was with my wife, and they asked me, and I said, "Could you come later in the evening when it was dark, when people wouldn't see?" And they said, "No problem." And then they came at 8.00 in the evening and took me in a Mercedes with black glass, and they took me to a private house in Ferizaj, on the second floor, and there there was a person - he was in plainclothes, a young lad about 35 - and he questioned me. They had information that I had ties with the Serbs. And they started interrogating me, and for three days -- and they didn't -- they didn't harass me. They gave me bread and they gave me a carton of Marlboro cigarettes, and nobody touched me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you released after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After three days, I was taken by car again, and they took me back to my uncle's, and they gave me a document with the stamp of the KLA and said that, "You are free and you don't have any problems with us, you can go out freely, but be careful because word has got about that you were mixed up in this business."

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you detained again by the KLA after that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this incident, a week later or maybe two, I can't be sure, they took me again, but these were men in KLA uniforms and masks. But they weren't really KLA members. They were merely a gang. And they put themselves -- they gave themselves out as KLA members. And they took me to a village and held me for a very long time and mistreated me. But their business was a different one which I wouldn't be able to understand myself. These were not members of the KLA, they were merely doing things in the name of the KLA, pretending. And the real KLA that took me the first time didn't bother me. They -- they didn't mistreat me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know they were merely a group and not KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could understand this because the KLA before, they came and they wanted information. But the other group -- but the other group was asking me about other problems which I'd had beforehand because of my wife and other problems of this kind. This was a different business at all. This was not the real KLA, they were just pretending to be the KLA. A lot of things -- a lot of people did things before the war and after the war, saying they were the KLA, looting and doing acts of misdeeds of various kinds.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, did you look for protection with NATO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went to NATO and asked -- and went -- I went to the NATO commander, but they said that they could not do anything for a single person. And they said they could guard my house, but I didn't agree to this. And that was the end of this matter. And they told me to go to Serbia along with the Serbian refugees who were going in that direction. But I didn't agree to this either, and I decided to go back to my own home, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you at some point advised to contact the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I contacted the Red Cross, and from there I went to Macedonia as a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the status of protected witness; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does that protection consist of? What form does the protection take?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said, what does that protection consist of, the protection that you say you have been given? Where is the protection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You'll have to reclarify it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me make it even clearer: What you have been provided in the form of protection as you are a protected witness? What protection has been given you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We know what the protection is because the order has been made. It's not a matter for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's -- there's no real need to protect me because I came here of my own free will. I can look after myself. I have come here to speak out, myself, and to point out the Serbian criminals who did these things, that's why I came here. I don't need any protection, I can look after myself. Because I didn't do these things, other people did, as I said before. Because for these reasons, I have been outlawed by my family, by my neighbours, by my friends, and my entire society, and that's why I have come here to tell the truth rather than rumours. And I've come here to dispel these rumours. That's why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. Now I'm not quite clear, Mr. May, in view of the fact that this witness of yours says that he doesn't need any protective measures, any protection, why is he then boxed in with this screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's been ordered to have the protection. Now, go on with some other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your statement that nothing has been promised you in connection with your providing testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to answer questions of this kind. I said before why I have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is your duty to answer that question regardless of whether you wish to do so or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just repeat the question so he can hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you saying that to the interpreters or to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said at the beginning of your testimony that nothing had been promised you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask anything from them, but they promised me such a thing and -- and I was offered security by the Court as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what were those certain things? You said "such a thing," that you were promised such a thing or certain things. Which things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They promised me -- didn't ask anything, but -- but I've come of my own free will, but the Court offered me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no further comment on these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, the question is this: Besides the security which you've been offered if you gave evidence, has anybody offered you anything else; money, anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No money. Well, they gave me cigarettes, and they -- a place to sleep and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where were you offered a place to sleep, food and all the rest? In which place, where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not a question which he has to answer. It's normal for the witnesses here to be offered somewhere to sleep, but where they sleep is not a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about The Hague. I mean outside The Hague, where you are located at present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were promised some things, and it says here in the transcript what you said a moment ago. Now, could you be so kind as to enumerate what things were offered you exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt with that. He said he was -- Were you offered anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They offered me nothing. I said before. Food, lodging, money for cigarettes, nothing else. And security.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: house. I have my own family. Nobody gave me a house. And I've never heard of anybody being given a house either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The name of the town can be redacted. Witness K5, don't mention the town again unless it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I think the accused has to be made aware that there are areas that he cannot touch in -- because of security of this witness and the protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he wants to ask any questions which might identify the witness, then we should go into closed session. So anything where he lives, anything of that sort, will be done in closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I want to hear from the witness what he's going to say in response to my questions. I'm not interested in his -- where he lives, his place. I don't -- I'm not interested in identifying him either, because he doesn't deserve being identified. He wrote himself in his statement that he was a thief, that he was a drunkard and a police informant, that he is a criminal in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't let's go over this again. Now, if you've got any questions which identify him or might identify him, they're to be asked in closed session. But let's move on. I think we've probably gone over this topic enough. If you want to put anything about his character that's in his statement, of course you can put it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all of that is in his statement, but we'll come to that. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Explain to me, please, how you got yourself into the situation of giving statements to the investigators. How did you come to give statements to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before I came here of my own accord. I wasn't forced to come here by anybody. I came here of my own accord from another country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. The question was: How did you come to give a statement to the investigators in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said before, I gave this statement myself. I came to the Tribunal myself, and I asked myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Earlier than that. You made a statement in October 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, just help us with this: How did you come to make the statement? Did somebody get in touch with you or did you get in touch with somebody? How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I contacted them myself. And the Red Cross was present too. And we went to a place - I don't want to mention the name of the town - and then I reported there myself and gave them some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you gave the statement, I assume that this is no secret because we can conclude that from your statement, you were in Macedonia; is that right? You were in a refugee camp there; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a refugee in a camp in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that through the Red Cross, which was in the camp, you came into contact with the investigators. Can we conclude that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was. I went with the Red Cross, and I reported to The Hague Tribunal there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And John Zdrilic, the investigator, had talks with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did he conduct the interviews in Macedonia or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, it says that the KLA deprived of their -- killed many Albanians who were in any way loyal to the Serb authorities during the war and afterwards. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I wasn't there, but I have heard from people. I don't know who they killed, but I've heard this from people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From people. Simply from people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard that from people. From your neighbours or from your friends or did you hear it when you were in Macedonia in the refugee camp perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard in the camp. I heard from people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there many people with you in that refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in your statement, you say quite specifically the names and surnames of many Albanians, your compatriots who allegedly were police informants; is that right? Are those names correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what names you mean here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the names that you state in your statement. I'll read them out later on, or I can do it now, if you want me to. Now, all these names you quoted, are they all the names or do you have more to give?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who killed them. I don't know who killed them. I said I've heard this. I have never seen these things, but I've heard that they killed people. I heard that they killed people, but I don't know whether it's true or not myself. I have no way of knowing because I didn't see this. I have told you the things that I have said, and I've told you the things that I have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you claim that you are afraid of KLA retaliation or that of some other Albanians. Why is that so? You are afraid that they will get their own back. That is what you say in your statement on page 2, in paragraph 2. Now, why is that so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid of the KLA because the KLA took me and held me for three days. I told you before. I have been frightened of other people who have said that this person has done such-and-such a thing. But as I said, I didn't do these things. These things were done by other people. They were done by the Serbian police. I didn't do them. That's why I've come here to tell the truth, to say what I have done and what I haven't done. I'm not frightened of anybody. I'm not frightened of the KLA or anybody else, and I've come myself to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. It says in paragraph 2, at the beginning of your statement -- there is the following sentence which you say is your own sentence, as you put: "I cannot live in Urosevac because I am afraid of the KLA's revenge or that of other Albanians." So as an Albanian, you explained that you cannot live in Urosevac because you are afraid that the KLA will take their revenge, as will perhaps other Albanians. Now you say something else. Will you explain to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In his witness statement, which is dated October 2000, he says that. We're now in 2002. Is it right, Mr. K5, that you were afraid, at one stage, of reprisals from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not by -- from the KLA. Before, I was afraid, as I mentioned before. I was scared of other people who had spread rumours that I had been working for the Black Hand, because the KLA took me, detained me, and they held me for three days, and if they had wanted to kill me, they would have done. But they didn't want to kill me because they knew who I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They took me and then released me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's past the time for an adjournment. We will adjourn now. Yes. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the 24th of April, 1992, the municipal court in Urosevac sentenced you to four months in prison, according to Article 165, on charges on theft, that is 11/90, dated the 24th of April, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I mean, there are court documents about this, but you claim that this is not correct; right? And is it correct that on the 9th of May, 1994, that is K604/92, the municipal court in Urosevac sentenced you to three months in prison, again on the basis of Article 165, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, again for robbery? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And is it correct that on the 5th of March, 1997, that is K1161/92, the municipal court in Urosevac sentenced you to three months in prison on the basis of Article 174/19 in relation to Article 19 for stealing a motor vehicle? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct either, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you accused of grave robbery in 1997, that is 15588/87, when you were accused of grave robbery, Article 165, paragraph 3 of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true either. These are false accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. And in 1989, number 278/89, Article 135 of the Criminal Code of Kosovo in 1989, were you accused of that or not? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Also -- also, there are charges that were brought against you, ten at that, for grave robbery, and they are recorded under number 519853821, 620, 613, 553, and 535, all in 1990, again according to Article 165 for grave robbery and also Article 173 for stealing a motor vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So for these ten offences of grave robbery and one offence of stealing a vehicle, do you know about the charges that were brought against you with regard to these particular offences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the accusations. I only know that Mitic and Crni burnt down the other buildings. I know that the KLA had invitation [as interpreted] about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Don't go off the point, please, Witness K5. You're just being asked about these allegations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As to the accusations, they're not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And were you accused -- there is a criminal report filed against you, number 8 from 1991, again related to Article 165, again grave robbery, the ten grave robberies related to 1990, and in 1991 there was also a grave robbery. Charges were pressed against you for that. Yes or no. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, again grave robbery and breaking into premises, again 143/ -- 434/91. That is the number of the criminal file. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1990 onwards, as I said earlier, I worked for Mitic. So I don't know anything about that. I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the criminal reports that were filed against you for grave robbery; 199, 286, 317, 334, 335, 390, 397, 415, 416, all of this dated 1991, again according to Article 166, that is again grave robbery, and also Article 174, that's a vehicle yet again. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that you also stole from a motor vehicle. That is 17 -- 781/91. Do you know about that? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I had -- I had my own motor vehicle at home. I had a car. I didn't need to steal one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 155/92, according to Article 165, again grave robbery. Do you know about that? This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know about that either. And what about 683, also in 1992, according to Article 174 in relation to Article 19 of the Criminal Code; do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the decision of the municipal prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness [sic] please read the numbers out slowly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Charges were brought against you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know of grave bodily injury from 1993? That is number 22, dated 1993. Charges were brought against you on account of that as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't found guilty of that at all. They know who it was. But I was -- I defended myself, and I was found not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Is that when you say that you were in prison for nine months? In your statement, you say that you were in prison for nine months and then you were set free after that. That's what you said. That's what you claimed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, I was nine months -- spent nine months in prison, but that was -- Azem Haliti and Bajgora were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not that grave bodily injury. It is later. All right. According to Article 220, paragraph 1, in 1993 also. Do you know anything about that? Is that incorrect as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, in 1995, that is number 341, and it's according to Article 168 of the Criminal Code of Serbia, robbery again. Do you know anything about that? Is that incorrect as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was working for Mitic at the time. Everything I did was Mitic's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether it is correct that you carried out these criminal offences, whether you committed them or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that I was working for -- under the orders of Mitic, not on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get to that as well. Do you remember the criminal report that was filed against you according to Article 54, paragraph 2, that is to say, attack upon body and life. That is criminal report number 585 from 1995 -- 1997.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. So all these criminal offences that I listed to you from 1990 onwards, all the way up to, as far as I can see here, until 1997, you don't know anything about this. All of this is incorrect. Is that your assertion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that from 1990 onwards, I was under the direction of Avdi and under the direction of Mitic, and that was when these things were -- these events took place and were committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. Why do you fear KLA revenge or revenge from other Albanians? That's what I asked you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't afraid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no need to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. He said he was not afraid of the KLA, because obviously he had things sorted out with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who are these other Albanians that you are afraid of? You haven't answered that part.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't afraid of the KLA. As I said, it was not a question of fear. For all the -- all the things that I was involved in and all the things I was accused of, rumours could spread among the population, among the people of Ferizaj. They would be -- I would be treated as an outlaw in society. I wasn't afraid of the KLA itself or of specific Albanians but of public opinion, that's why. I have come here to tell the truth, to tell exactly who did what. This is justice, to come here and tell before justice what happened. There were Serbian police and inspectors who gave me their orders, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've said that. That is your statement. Tell me, now, on the basis of what did these rumours start circulating around Urosevac that, with other people, you were killing people for money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were the police who instigated such rumours. The police themselves were spreading rumours. They said that I had done such things to accuse the -- so that the Albanians would take revenge. They said that I had killed people for money, but that's not true. I didn't kill anyone for money, for money or without money. They were killing people simply because they were Albanians, it wasn't a question of money. There were civilians being killed; women and children, old people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You described some cases that you took part in. Do you claim that you did not take part in a single killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take part in any killing. I accompanied them, but my hands were never covered in blood. I accompanied Mitic, but I never took part myself in the killings, but I knew who did do the killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you were present when these killings took place, these murders that you say allegedly took place. So you were there on the spot, you actually saw the murders? Did these murders take place right in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them myself. I heard of the order -- about the orders, but I didn't see the event taking place with my own eyes. For example, in Nerodime, when we were in the village of Nerodime --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you see at least one murder, one killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we went on the Pleshina Street to mine the Gimi motel, I saw Dimitri there with a silencer on his gun, and there were two people, one in front of us and one ten metres behind us in a car, and he was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you saw with your very own eyes. What kind of rifle is this with a silencer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of rifle, you mean? It was an automatic weapon. It was black. The colour was black. And there were other rifles. There was a M45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about this rifle with the silencer. What kind of a rifle was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly -- the exact mark because I didn't have it in my hands. I just heard it. Mitic had given me one weapon, and if I were to see a picture of it, I would recognise it, but I don't know the name of the mark, the brand mark of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the weapon that you recognised over here when you were pointing out a rifle, saying that they were armed with that type of weapon? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That's a different thing. That's -- these were automatic weapons but with silencers. They were black coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know which type this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. What I don't know, I don't know. I can't lie and tell you things I don't know. If you'd show me a picture, I can tell you which it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You say no. Was it similar to the one you pointed out? Was it that size, bigger, smaller?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Smaller. Shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So is this one murder that you saw with your very own eyes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, two murders. In the Pleshina Street. There were two people. Two people were killed; one in front of us and one ten metres behind us, another person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb police, Dimitri of the Serbs. He was a policeman at the police station in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On page 2 of your statement, in paragraph 3, you say that you were expelled from the school of the interior in Vucitrn because you did not attend classes and because of some other things. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That took place in 1994, 1995. I was at the police academy in Vucitrn, police school, but I wasn't a good student. It was 1984, 1985, I think, and I wasn't good at shooting, as good as the other students. One of them was a Serb from Decan there. And we were thrown out of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How old were you in 1984?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was 19, 20. About 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you born? What year?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born in 1969, 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 1969. So in 1984, you were 15 years old. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's when they threw you out of school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember. And the year, the exact year, I don't really remember. You have a lot of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What are these other things? You say they threw you out of school because you did not attend classes and now you say you were not a good student, et cetera, et cetera, and also on account of some other things. What are the other things on account of which they threw you out of school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any other things. Well, just that I wasn't a very good student. I didn't learn well, and I wasn't good in the exercises, and so they expelled me from school. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there's no other thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you write this down in your statement that there were other things when there are no other things?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of the other things was that I didn't attend class regularly and that I wasn't very good. I wasn't good at learning, and that's why they expelled me. They all got together and had a meeting and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When did your father die? When did you father die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father died in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a police inspector; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go into private session while these questions go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This man Avdi Musa, later on, as you say, was killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who killed him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed because he upset a lot of people. Like the business of my family. He was a criminal, and he really had it out for the Albanians. He only wanted to cause trouble. He was a -- he was a rapist. He was everything. And he upset somebody, and somebody killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say he was killed because he caused problems to your family. Does that mean that you killed him or a member of your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I didn't kill him. I don't get my hands dirty in things like that. He was killed by God. I didn't kill him. How would I get mixed up in this sort of thing? Maybe the police killed him. Maybe the Serbian police killed him because he knew a lot of things about the Serbs. So they might have killed him. He killed a lot of Albanians. Like Bajram --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K5 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a collaborator with the Serbs, and the Serbs may have killed him. That may be the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K5, despite the questions, could you keep your answers as short as possible, and we'll get on more quickly that way. Just concentrate, if you would, on answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Azem Haliti still lives in Urosevac, according to what you wrote here. How is that possible when he worked for the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Azem Haliti was as a SUP inspector and now he's under house arrest. But not because of the KLA. But he doesn't dare go out because he mistreated people. He beat his own neighbours. He took in people, and he took 2.000 or 3.000 marks in bribes just to issue passports. How can he dare go out of his house? People are looking for him because he beat their fathers and for taking 3.000 marks for a passport. And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request the witness repeat his answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll go on from there. Let's move on. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you claim, on page 3, paragraph 1, that you started secretly working for the police already in 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1990, not from 1990 -- not from 1992, from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, which is it, what it says in your statement or are you correcting your statement now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K5 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not correcting it.
